data.intent: Get fully prepared for a fintech job interview next week: a day-by-day plan, company and domain research, a story bank, practice tracking, logistics, and reference links.

suggestions.title: 7-day interview prep plan
suggestions.reason: A day-by-day roadmap so the week before the interview is structured, not scrambled

content.text: Interview prep plan
Goal: walk in able to explain the company, the role, and why I'm a fit in under two minutes each.
Days 7-5: Research and foundations
Read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Complete the company research page (products, customers, competitors, news)
Look up the interviewers on LinkedIn
Review core fintech concepts in the study table
Days 4-3: Stories and practice
Write 6 STAR stories covering the main competencies
Draft and rehearse a 90-second 'Tell me about yourself'
Do a timed practice run of the top 10 questions
Practice technical or case problems if the role needs them
Days 2-1: Polish and logistics
Run a full mock interview with a friend or record yourself
Finalize questions to ask the interviewers
Test video link, camera, mic, or plan the commute
Lay out clothes and print or open your resume
After the interview
Send thank-you emails within 24 hours, referencing one specific topic from each conversation
Jot down what went well and what to improve

Past

Future
Why this fintech company and this role are the natural next step.

content.text: Questions for interviewers

Business and strategy
How does regulation shape your roadmap over the next year?
What is the biggest challenge the company is working through right now?
Culture and next steps
How do teams make decisions when speed and compliance pull in different directions?
What are the next steps and timeline for the process?

content.text: Property overview

Rent policy
Rent is due on the 1st of each month.
Grace period: 5 days. Late fee applies after the grace period (check local limits).

Maintenance process
Tenant reports the issue in writing with photos.
Log it in the Maintenance requests table and set a priority.
Emergencies are handled the same day; normal requests within 3-5 days.
Confirm the fix with the tenant and record the cost.
Decisions & notes

content.text: Monthly checklist
Start of month
Add this month's rent charges to Rent payments
Send rent reminders to tenants
Pay mortgage, property tax and insurance as due
Mid month
Follow up on late or partial payments
Review open maintenance requests and update statuses
End of month
Log expenses and file receipts
Update the rent collected and outstanding figures
Check for leases expiring in the next 90 days

Smoke and CO detectors tested

Four travelers, two weeks, three bases. Goal: a mix of big-city energy, culture and downtime, with a pace that works for the whole family.

Days 6–10: Kyoto (Fushimi Inari, Arashiyama, Gion, day trip to Nara)
Days 11–14: Osaka (Dotonbori, Osaka Castle, Universal Studios, fly home)

At least one rest or light day after every three busy days
One signature experience per city that everyone picks together
Keep luggage moves to a minimum: use takkyubin to forward big bags between cities
Decisions to make
Confirm travel dates and flights
Decide: JR Pass vs. individual Shinkansen tickets
Decide: Universal Studios Japan, yes or no
Choose family-room hotels vs. an apartment rental

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

This brief outlines the plan to move our existing team wiki into PlexiiWrite. It is meant to align the team on why we are doing this, what is and is not included, how the work will unfold, and what could go wrong. Details marked in brackets still need to be confirmed before the brief is circulated.
Goals
The migration should leave us with a single, trusted home for team knowledge that is easier to find, easier to edit, and easier to keep current. Specifically, we want to:
Move all content we choose to keep into PlexiiWrite with its structure and links intact.
Retire the old wiki so there is one source of truth and no drifting duplicates.
Make sure every team member can find, read, and edit pages in PlexiiWrite without extra help.
Use the move as a chance to clear out outdated and duplicate pages instead of carrying them over.
Success will be measured by [success criteria, for example: percentage of pages migrated, old wiki set to read-only by a given date, team sign-off after a trial period].
Scope

In scope are the pages, attachments, and page hierarchy in the current wiki [name of current wiki tool], along with a content audit to decide what to keep, archive, or delete. Also in scope are setting up the workspace structure and permissions in PlexiiWrite, short guidance for the team on how to use it, and redirecting or clearly flagging the old wiki once the move is complete.

Out of scope are rewriting content beyond light formatting fixes, integrating PlexiiWrite with other tools unless required for launch [confirm any required integrations], and migrating content that lives outside the wiki, such as shared drives or chat history.
Timeline
The plan runs in five phases. Dates and durations are to be set once the size of the wiki is known.
Audit and planning: inventory existing pages, decide what to keep, and agree on the new structure. [dates]
Workspace setup: build the structure, set permissions, and test an import with a small sample. [dates]
Migration: move content in batches, fix formatting and broken links, and check each batch. [dates]
Review and trial: the team uses PlexiiWrite alongside the old wiki, which is frozen to new edits, and reports problems. [dates]
Cutover and retirement: switch over, set the old wiki to read-only, and archive it. [dates]
The project owner is [owner name], with [reviewers or content owners] responsible for checking their own sections.
Risks
Content may not import cleanly, leading to broken formatting, lost attachments, or dead links. A sample import early on and a link check after each batch will surface this sooner.
Without a clear freeze on edits, the old wiki and PlexiiWrite could diverge during the move. We will announce a freeze date and stick to it.
Team members may keep using the old wiki out of habit. Clear communication, brief guidance, and setting the old wiki to read-only at cutover should address this.
The audit could take longer than expected if page owners are unclear. Naming a content owner for each major section early will help.
Permissions may be set incorrectly, exposing sensitive pages or blocking access. Permissions should be reviewed before the trial begins.
Next Steps
Confirm the owner and reviewers, size up the existing wiki, fix the dates above, and schedule a kickoff with the team.

# Support Agent Onboarding Guide

## Welcome to the team

This guide is your map for the first week. It covers what you will do each day, the tools you will use, and how we handle escalations when a customer's problem is beyond what you can solve alone. Read it once through before your first day, then keep it open as a reference.

Nobody expects you to know everything in week one. What we do expect is that you ask questions early, document what you learn, and never leave a customer without a clear next step. If something in this guide is out of date or unclear, tell [onboarding owner] so the next person has a better version.

## Your first week

The plan below is a starting point. Your manager, [manager name], will adjust the pace based on how things go.

### Day 1: Get set up and get oriented

Today is about access and context. You should finish the day able to log in to everything and explain what our product does and who uses it.

- Confirm you can log in to every tool listed in the Tools section below, and flag anything missing to [IT or access contact].
- Meet your manager and your onboarding buddy, [buddy name].
- Walk through the product as a customer would, from sign-up to the core workflow. Take notes on anything confusing, because new customers will find it confusing too.
- Read our support principles and tone guidelines at [link to guidelines].

### Day 2: Learn how tickets flow

Spend the morning learning how a ticket moves from arrival to resolution, including how it is categorized, prioritized and assigned. In the afternoon, shadow your buddy on live tickets and ask why they made each choice.

- Review the saved replies and help center articles most often used, found at [link].
- Read ten to fifteen recently resolved tickets chosen by your buddy, covering a mix of easy and difficult cases.
- Learn our priority levels and the response targets attached to each: [priority levels and response targets].

### Day 3: Start answering with a safety net

You will begin drafting replies to real tickets. Your buddy or a designated reviewer will check each reply before it is sent, so you can learn without risk to the customer.

- Take simple, low-priority tickets first.
- Use the help center and internal documentation to verify every answer before you send it.
- Note every question you could not answer. These are your learning list.

### Day 4: Send replies independently on routine tickets

If your reviewer is comfortable with your drafts, you will start sending replies on routine tickets without pre-approval. Reviews continue on a sample basis. Today is also the day to practice your first escalations, with your buddy watching, using the process described below.

### Day 5: Review and plan

Meet with [manager name] to look back on the week. Come with your learning list, a view on which topics you feel solid on and which you do not, and any suggestions for improving this guide. Together you will set goals for weeks two through four, such as [30-day goals].

## Tools

You will spend most of your time in a handful of systems. Each one has a specific purpose, so use the right one for the job.

- The helpdesk, [ticketing tool], is where all customer conversations live. Every customer interaction should be recorded here, even if it started somewhere else.
- The internal knowledge base, [knowledge base tool], holds troubleshooting steps, policies and product documentation. Check it before asking a colleague, and update it when you find something wrong or missing.
- Team chat, [chat tool], is for quick questions and coordination. Use the channel [support channel name] for general questions and [incident channel name] for live incidents.
- The admin or back-office tool, [admin tool], lets you look up accounts and see what a customer sees. Access is limited to what your role needs, so treat customer data with care and only view accounts you have a reason to view.
- The bug and engineering tracker, [tracker name], is where product defects and feature requests are logged. Search it before filing anything new, to avoid duplicates.
- Other tools you may need, such as [phone or video tool], [status page tool] and [CRM, if used], will be introduced as they become relevant.

## Handling tickets well

Before the specifics of escalation, a few habits apply to every ticket.

Read the whole conversation history before replying, so the customer never has to repeat themselves. Answer the question they actually asked, and then anticipate the obvious next one. Write in plain language, avoid internal jargon, and be honest about what you do not know. If you cannot fix something right away, say what happens next and when the customer will hear from us again, then make sure that follow-up really happens.

Never guess at an answer, and never promise something you cannot confirm, such as a refund, a feature date or a fix timeline, unless policy explicitly lets you. Saying "let me confirm that and come back to you by [time]" is always acceptable.

## How we handle escalations

An escalation is the handoff of a ticket to someone with more expertise, authority or access. Escalating is not a failure. Holding on to a ticket you cannot solve, while the customer waits, is the real mistake.

### When to escalate

Escalate when one or more of the following is true:

- You have followed the documented troubleshooting steps and the problem is not resolved.
- The issue looks like a product bug or an outage.
- The request needs permissions or authority you do not have, such as exceptions to policy, refunds above your limit of [refund limit], or account changes you cannot make.
- The ticket involves security, privacy, legal threats, or a possible data exposure.
- The customer is at risk of leaving or has asked for a manager, and you cannot settle the situation yourself.
- You are unsure, and getting it wrong would be costly to the customer.

Anything involving security or a possible data exposure should be escalated immediately, without first trying to solve it yourself.

### Where escalations go

Our escalation paths are listed below. Use the one that matches the type of issue.

- Product defects and technical problems go to [technical escalation team or channel].
- Billing and refund exceptions go to [billing owner or team].
- Security, privacy and legal matters go to [security or legal contact].
- Customer relationship issues, including complaints and requests for a manager, go to [team lead or manager name].
- Live outages go to [on-call contact or incident process].

### How to write an escalation

A good escalation lets the next person act without going back to you or the customer for basics. Include the following in your internal note or handoff message:

- A one-sentence summary of the problem and who is affected.
- The customer's account details or identifier, and a link to the ticket.
- What the customer expected and what actually happened.
- Steps to reproduce the problem, if you have them, plus screenshots, error messages or logs.
- What you have already tried and what you ruled out.
- The impact, such as how many users, whether work is blocked, and any deadline the customer has mentioned.
- What you have already told the customer, so nobody contradicts it.
- What you need from the person receiving the escalation, whether that is a fix, a decision or an answer.

### Setting severity

Choose a severity level honestly. Overstating urgency makes it harder for real emergencies to be noticed. Our levels are [severity level definitions], with target response times of [response times per severity level].

### After you escalate

You still own the customer relationship. Tell the customer that the issue has been passed to a specialist, what to expect and when they will next hear from us. Set yourself a reminder to check progress at [follow-up interval]. If the escalation has not been picked up within the target time, follow up in [channel], and if there is still no response, go to [team lead or manager name]. When the issue is resolved, confirm with the customer, close the loop on the ticket, and add what you learned to the knowledge base if it was not already there.

## Who to ask

Your first stop for everyday questions is your buddy, [buddy name]

Team chat, [chat tool], is for quick questions and coordination. Use the channel [support channel name] for general questions and [incident channel name] for live incidents.

The admin or back-office tool, [admin tool], lets you look up accounts and see what a customer sees. Access is limited to what your role needs, so treat customer data with care and only view accounts you have a reason to view.
The bug and engineering tracker, [tracker name], is where product defects and feature requests are logged. Search it before filing anything new, to avoid duplicates.
Other tools you may need, such as [phone or video tool], [status page tool] and [CRM, if used], will be introduced as they become relevant.
Handling tickets well
Before the specifics of escalation, a few habits apply to every ticket.

Read the whole conversation history before replying, so the customer never has to repeat themselves. Answer the question they actually asked, and then anticipate the obvious next one. Write in plain language, avoid internal jargon, and be honest about what you do not know. If you cannot fix something right away, say what happens next and when the customer will hear from us again, then make sure that follow-up really happens.

An escalation is the handoff of a ticket to someone with more expertise, authority or access. Escalating is not a failure. Holding on to a ticket you cannot solve, while the customer waits, is the real mistake.

You have followed the documented troubleshooting steps and the problem is not resolved.

Billing and refund exceptions go to [billing owner or team].
Security, privacy and legal matters go to [security or legal contact].

A good escalation lets the next person act without going back to you or the customer for basics. Include the following in your internal note or handoff message:
A one-sentence summary of the problem and who is affected.

What you have already told the customer, so nobody contradicts it.

Choose a severity level honestly. Overstating urgency makes it harder for real emergencies to be noticed. Our levels are [severity level definitions], with target response times of [response times per severity level].
After you escalate

You still own the customer relationship. Tell the customer that the issue has been passed to a specialist, what to expect and when they will next hear from us. Set yourself a reminder to check progress at [follow-up interval]. If the escalation has not been picked up within the target time, follow up in [channel], and if there is still no response, go to [team lead or manager name]. When the issue is resolved, confirm with the customer, close the loop on the ticket, and add what you learned to the knowledge base if it was not already there.

You draft a complete, well-structured business document in Markdown. Put the document title on the FIRST line as a single H1 (# Title). Then write the body using ## for section headings, prose paragraphs, and - for bullets only where a real list is warranted. Aim for a genuinely useful first draft the user will edit. Reply with raw Markdown only: no preamble, no code fences. Write in plain, confident, human prose. Do not use em dashes or emoji. Do not use a bold label followed by a colon as a heading substitute; write real sentences. Ground every specific in what you were given. Write the prose, the structure and ordinary domain knowledge freely, because that is the draft and an empty skeleton is no use. But never present an invented specific as fact: no statistic, study finding, quotation, price, date or market figure you cannot source, and no detail about the reader's own world (their people, customers, revenue, tools, deadlines or past decisions) that the request did not supply. Where such a specific is genuinely needed and was not supplied, write a short bracketed placeholder like [launch date] or [owner name] instead of a plausible guess. A placeholder costs the user seconds to fill in; an invented figure they do not notice can reach a customer. Prefer a shorter, fully grounded draft over a fuller one that is partly fiction.

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. This session is about a small skill that saves the whole team a lot of time: writing a bug report that someone else can act on without chasing you for details.

slides.title: Why a good report matters
bullets: A clear report gets fixed faster
It saves the developer a round of questions
It helps triage decide how urgent the bug is
It leaves a useful record for anyone who hits the same issue later
slides.notes: Every unclear report costs a back-and-forth before work can even start. A good report lets the person picking it up begin straight away. Think of the report as a handoff to someone who was not there when it happened.

slides.title: Start with a specific title and summary
bullets: Name the problem, not just the area
Say what happened and where
Avoid vague titles like "Search is broken"
Better: "Search returns no results when the query contains an apostrophe"
Use one or two sentences for the summary
slides.notes: The title is what people see in lists and search results, so make it carry real information. Compare the vague example with the specific one on the slide. If you can only describe the bug vaguely, that is a sign to investigate a little more before filing.

slides.title: Give steps to reproduce
bullets: Number each step in the order you did it
Include the starting state, such as being logged in or a specific page
Include the exact input you used
Keep only the steps that matter
Note whether it happens every time or only sometimes
slides.notes: Reproduction steps are the most valuable part of any report. Write them so a colleague could follow them cold. If the bug is intermittent, say so plainly and describe how often you saw it, since that tells the developer where to look.

slides.title: Expected versus actual, plus context
bullets: State what you expected to happen
State what actually happened
Attach a screenshot, recording or log excerpt
Include the environment: browser or device, app version, operating system
Mention anything recent that might be related
slides.notes: Spelling out expected and actual behavior removes any doubt about what you consider wrong. Evidence like a screenshot or error message beats a description. Environment details often turn out to be the key to why only some people see the problem.

slides.title: Before you file: a quick checklist
bullets: Search for an existing report first
Reproduce the bug at least once more
Confirm the title is specific
Check that the steps work from a clean start
Add severity or impact if you know it
Remove passwords and personal data from attachments
slides.notes: Run through this list every time until it becomes habit. Checking for duplicates and removing sensitive data are the two steps people skip most often. Finish by inviting questions, and point people to [team bug tracker or template link] for the standard template.

Annual plans are refunded pro rata. That means we refund the portion of the year you have not used, and we keep the portion you have. If you cancel within the first 30 days, you receive a full refund instead.
